summary: Superconducting transmons on a silicon chip were monitored at 1 μs temporal resolution using co-integrated microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKIDs) to study ionizing radiation effects. No correlation was found between TLS scrambling events and cosmic-ray-induced ionizing radiation across 371 TLS events and 18,454 radiation triggers, suggesting previous charge-jump correlations arise from lower-energy processes.
motivation: Two-level-system (TLS) dynamics and qubit relaxation degradation during ionizing radiation events have been reported previously, but with timing resolution limited to milliseconds or relying on charge-sensitive measurements with energy thresholds well below cosmic-ray energies, leaving ambiguity about causation.
method: MKIDs fabricated from 30 nm granular aluminum with 250 kHz linewidth achieved 1 μs response time and ~40 keV energy threshold for ionizing radiation detection. Transmons with niobium capacitors and aluminum junctions were simultaneously measured during cosmic-ray exposure at sea level. Enhanced relaxation and excitation dynamics relative to MKID-detected radiation events were extracted by averaging over 3731 (90 h) and 606 (17 h) events respectively.
result: Qubit $T_1$ recovery after radiation events exhibited characteristic time $13 ± 1$ μs following a quasiparticle trapping model ($\dot{n}_{qp} = -s n_{qp}$), corresponding to peak quasiparticle density $85^{+9}_{-8}$ μm$^{-3}$ or $240$ μm$^{-3}$MeV$^{-1}$. Excess excitations ($|0\rangle \to |1\rangle$) recovered with $8.3^{+1.7}_{-1.2}$ μs, attributed to energetic quasiparticles diffusing from niobium onto aluminum leads before thermalization; proximity effect of niobium reduced recovery times compared to all-aluminum devices ($25$–$5$ ms in literature).
